rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Linear momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ measures 'quantity of motion'. Newton's second law in its general form is $\vec{F} = d\vec{p}/dt$, and integrating it over a collision interval gives the impulse–momentum theorem $\vec{J} = \int F\,dt = \Delta\vec{p}$ — impulse is the area under the force–time graph.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Momentum: $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ [kg·m/s]
Second law (general): $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$; constant mass: $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$
Impulse (constant force): $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t$; general: $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ (area under $F$–$t$)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Isolated System Requirement:** Momentum conservation ($\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$) holds strictly only when the net *external* force on the system is zero. External forces like gravity, friction, or applied pushes must be absent or balanced.  ·  **Collisions vs. Continuous Interaction:** In a collision, the interaction is brief and impulsive; internal forces dominate. In continuous interactions (e.g., rocket propulsion), momentum is conserved at each instant, but mass changes must be tracked using the variable-mass form $F = dp/dt$.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: In rebound problems the velocity CHANGES SIGN — $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$, not the difference. The commonest numerical error.  ·  Note 2: Quote impulse in N·s and momentum in kg·m/s — numerically identical, and examiners check units.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1 (recoil): a 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 300 m/s — recoil speed $= \frac{0.02 \times 300}{5} = 1.2$ m/s backward.  ·  Example 2 (kicking): a footballer gives a 0.45 kg ball at rest a speed of 20 m/s in 0.05 s — impulse 9 N·s, average force 180 N.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.  ·  ❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Compute impulses for stop, rebound and deflect cases with explicit signs.  ·  Task 2: Extract final velocities from three force–time pulses (rectangle, triangle, trapezium).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Rebounds: add the speeds in $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$ — sign flip doubles the effect.  ·  Trick 2: 'Soft landing' MCQs: longer $\Delta t$ ⇒ smaller $F$ ⇒ pick the option that stretches the time.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Define linear momentum and impulse, and state the relation between them.  ·  Q2. Show that Newton's second law can be written as $F = dp/dt$ and state when this reduces to $F = ma$.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: Theory answers should state BOTH $J = F\Delta t$ and $J = \Delta p$ and connect them — one-line answers lose marks.  ·  Exam Tip 2: In numericals, convert grams to kg and quote directions ('opposite to initial motion') with magnitudes.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Momentum as the fundamental 'quantity of motion' vector $m\vec{v}$.  ·  Concept 2: General second law $F = dp/dt$ and its constant-mass reduction.  ·  Concept 3: Impulse as the time integral of force — area under $F$–$t$ — equal to momentum change.  ·  Concept 4: Force–time trade-off: $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$ and safety engineering.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Momentum is a vector — always assign signs/directions before computing $\Delta p$.  ·  Impulse and momentum share units (N·s = kg·m/s); impulse is the area under the force–time graph.  ·  For a FIXED momentum change, force and time trade off: $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$.  ·  $F = dp/dt$ is the general second law — essential for variable-mass (rocket) problems.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Airbags, crumple zones, helmets and safety nets are all impulse engineering: stretch the stopping time, cut the peak force, keep $\Delta p$ fixed.  ·  The impulse–momentum theorem explains why follow-through matters in sports — prolonging contact time increases delivered impulse and exit speed.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. A 0.3 kg ball moving at 15 m/s is hit back along the same path at 25 m/s. Find the impulse delivered.  ·  Q4. Explain, using the impulse–momentum theorem, why a crumple zone reduces injury in a crash.  ·  Q5. From a given force–time graph (triangle), determine the final velocity of the struck body.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: Graph-reading impulse questions: label the base and height you used to compute the area.  ·  Exam Tip 4: Safety-device explanations score full marks only with the chain: fixed $\Delta p$ → longer $\Delta t$ → smaller $F_{avg}$.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3 (graph): a rectangular $F$–$t$ pulse of 250 N lasting 0.04 s delivers $J = 10$ N·s — a 2 kg cart leaves at 5 m/s.  ·  Example 4 (safety): the same 4000 kg·m/s car momentum change stopped in 0.1 s (rigid wall) means 40 kN; in 0.5 s (crumple zone) only 8 kN — five times gentler.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The SI unit of impulse is: → C  ·  A 2 kg ball at 10 m/s bounces back at 10 m/s. The impulse magnitude is: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.  ·  **Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J).  ·  **Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Recoil and variable-mass motion as momentum bookkeeping.  ·  Impulse–momentum theorem: $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$  ·  Average force: $F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Kinetic Energy Distinction:** Momentum is conserved in *all* isolated collisions (elastic or inelastic). Kinetic energy is conserved *only* in perfectly elastic collisions. In inelastic collisions, some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation energy.  ·  Momentum conservation holds in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.  ·  Recoil problems are momentum bookkeeping: $M V + m v = 0$ from rest.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.  ·  ❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.  ·  ❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.  ·  Example 5 (jump landing): a 60 kg jumper hitting the ground at 6 m/s stops in 0.3 s with stiff legs (1200 N extra) vs 0.9 s with bent knees (400 N extra).  ·  Note 3: For force–time graphs, rectangular pulses are $F\Delta t$; triangular pulses are $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note 4: When a question says 'average force', it means $\Delta p/\Delta t$ — the constant force delivering the same impulse.  ·  Note 1: Impulse units (N·s) and momentum units (kg·m/s) are identical — that is the theorem speaking.  ·  Note 2: Momentum is directional: a rebound doubles the magnitude change versus a stop at the same speeds.
